chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 391 to 400, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade of the return (மறுதரவுப் பத்து): the household bribes the crow to caw the eloped girl home, asks the mother whether her daughter has come, says that the loveless right has shown grace; the man brings the girl through the burnt wasteland to his hill country, decks her hair and enters his town with her as an evening guest; she sends word to her companions; the mother blesses the road, proposes to divide the rites with the youth's house, and the message comes that the couple arrive today.

391.reading: The speaker promises the small black crow of flawless feathers a meal of raw flesh and fresh fat, served in a gold-worked bowl for it to share with its loving kin, if it will caw so that the girl of the few lovely tresses comes home with the youth of the fierce, victorious spear.
391.nuance: The crow's cawing was the household's sign that a guest was on the way; here the reward is offered before the sign, so the meal is a bribe to the omen rather than thanks for it. Promising a gold bowl to a crow measures the household's longing.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl who left with the youth is awaited home

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the mother or foster mother speaks to the crow; the speaker is not named

392.reading: Seeing her shoulders, which have lost their bamboo-like beauty, and her brow, whose fresh glow the sun's heat has destroyed, the girl tells her friend not to grieve, for grieving would bring pain without end, since she came with the man of the good hill country.
392.nuance: The wasted shoulders and sun-burned brow are the road's marks on a girl who has come back; the speaker refuses pity because she chose the journey, and the hill country of the man, not the burnt road, is what she names last. Who speaks to whom is not certain: the friend may be the speaker and the girl the one addressed as தோழி.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has come back from the sun-scorched road with her man

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; on the likelier reading the returned girl answers her friend's pity

393.reading: Someone asks the mother, who wasted under grief when the girl left and quarrelled with right and blamed it, whether her daughter has come, as a safeguard for her anguished heart, with the youth of fierce strength and white spear walking ahead.
393.nuance: The question pictures the mother at her lowest, blaming அறம் itself for the loss, and offers the return as the remedy for that charge; the youth walking in front is the sign of a lawful homecoming rather than a flight. அண்கணாட்டி is a rare word, read here as a name for the mother.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter who left is asked after as returning with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; someone of the household or town, perhaps the foster mother, questions the mother

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes and timid look

394.reading: The speaker says that the loveless right, which with its ignoble ways had caused bewildering grief, has surely shown grace after all, for it has brought before them the small-browed young girl of lovely few tresses who crossed the hot wasteland and whose glance outdid the great innocent doe; come and see.
394.nuance: The same அறம் that the household had called loveless (அன்பில் அறன்) is now said to have shown grace: the return reverses the verdict on the moral order itself. The doe is not likened but defeated (அலைத்த), the girl's look troubling the very creature it would be compared with.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has crossed the hot wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the mother calls the household (வம்மே) to see the returned girl

395.reading: The man tells the young girl that they have crossed the cruel, hard wasteland where the long flame of a fire born in dry bamboo and fanned by wind roars in the clefts and caves, and bids her walk slowly now toward their hill country, with its high dark groves where a roaring waterfall comes down mixed with blossoms.
395.nuance: The danger is named only as past (தீர்ந்தனம்), and the man's word is to slow down, not to hurry; the fire in the bamboo and the flower-laden waterfall set the two lands side by side, the road of paalai behind and his kurinji home ahead.

thinai_evidence.note: the couple have crossed the wasteland on the elopement road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the man speaks to the girl as they near his country

396.reading: The man bids the girl rest her weariness from the wasteland slowly, for as long as it takes him to pluck the golden clusters of the tiger-spotted vengai and set them in her hair, and then they will enter their rock-famed town as evening guests.
396.nuance: The plucking of flowers is a pretext that lets her rest without being told she is tired, and it makes her entry into his town an adorned one. She arrives not as a runaway but as a guest at nightfall (எல் விருந்து), the honoured status a newcomer is received with.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is weary from the wasteland crossed with her man

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the man speaks to the girl at the edge of his town

397.reading: The speaker asks those hurrying on ahead to tell her sweet-smiling companions beforehand that she is coming across the wasteland, where the red wild dog with shaggy drooping neck passes by without seizing the young piglet.
397.nuance: The companions she left behind are the first to be told of her return. The wild dog that spares the piglet makes the road gentle and is traditionally read as a sign of forbearance at home; it is kept as scene, since nothing in the poem ties the dog's act to what a person of the situation does (iraicchi condition 2). விரந்த is read as விரைந்த; the speaker may be the girl speaking of herself in the third person.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is on her way back across the wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the girl, on the likelier reading, speaks to travellers going ahead to her town

398.reading: The speaker wishes the wasteland may be very sweet for the returning pair, with many fruits ripened that even the birds have not found and broad pools standing that even the young deer have not known, and tells her friend that though she weeps each time she thinks of it, the town is lonelier still.
398.nuance: The wish for a kind road, with food and water no creature has yet taken, is reserved wholly for the travellers; the speaker's own grief is then outweighed by the town's, so the girl's absence is a loss to the whole place. நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் is the formula of the mother's lament in this poet's decade 38.

thinai_evidence.note: the wish is for the wasteland road

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the mother, by the lament formula, speaks to a woman she calls தோழி

399.reading: The speaker asks what harm there would be in telling the mother who bore the lying youth of the victorious spear and the anklet-bright feet: even if you perform the anklet-removal in your house, let the good wedding be done in ours.
399.nuance: The anklet-removal (சிலம்பு கழீஇ), the rite that ends a girl's maidenhood, and the wedding are treated as two rites the two houses can divide; the girl's side concedes the first to the youth's house and claims the second. The youth is still called a liar (பொய்வல் காளை) in the very message that proposes the settlement.

thinai_evidence.note: the families settle the rites after the girl went with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; the girl's mother, on the likelier reading, speaks of a message to the youth's mother

comparisons.tenor: the swaying creeper embracing the tree

400.reading: Word has come that in the season of summer's plenty, when the maravam trees stand like warriors and the swaying creeper, like women, embraces and shakes them, the girl, united in love with the youth of the fierce, victorious spear and fine anklet, will come home today.
400.nuance: The tree and creeper repeat the couple in the season's own figures, the warrior-like tree held by the woman-like creeper, but the similes are stated with அன்ன, so the scene is open comparison, not ullurai. அரும்பதம் கொண்ட பெரும்பத வேனில் is hard to fix: a summer that holds rare food in plenty, or a summer of great heat.

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (மறுதரவுப் பத்து) places the poem at the couple's return after the elopement; someone of the household, perhaps the foster mother, announces the message

links.note: Both reward the crow whose cawing brings a guest (விருந்துவரக் கரைந்த காக்கை; வரக்கரைந் தீமே): Kuruntokai's friend after the man has come, Ainkurunuru's speaker before the girl has.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai pays the crow afterwards and calls even seven bowls too little, while Ainkurunuru promises meat in a gold bowl in advance, so together they show the crow offering working as a bargain struck with the omen on either side of the homecoming.

links.note: 376 is the mother's curse on the fate without right (அறனில் பால்) that sent the girl; 393 describes her from outside as one who quarrelled with right and blamed it (அறம்புலந்து பழிக்கும்).
links.teaches: The curse the mother speaks in her own voice in decade 38 is named in decade 40 as a quarrel with அறம் that the daughter's return is meant to heal, so the poet frames the lament as a dispute with the moral order that the homecoming settles.

links.note: 376 calls the joining that sent the girl away a fate without right; 394 says the loveless right has after all shown grace (அன்பில் அறனும் அருளிற்று).
links.teaches: The same poet lets the verdict on அறம் turn with events, loveless when the girl left and gracious when she returns, so in these decades the moral order is judged by its outcome for the household rather than held fixed.

links.note: Both are the man's words to the girl at the end of the road as his own place comes into view (எம் சிறு நல் ஊரே; நம் மலைகெழு நாட்டே); Natrinai urges her on (ஏகுதி) because the day is ending, Ainkurunuru tells her to go slowly (மென்மெல ஏகுமதி) because the wasteland is behind them.
links.teaches: The same command to walk on means hurry in Natrinai and go slowly in Ainkurunuru, so the man's care at the journey's end is shaped by what threatens, the coming night or the danger just passed.

links.note: In both the man decks the eloping girl's hair with forest flowers, maraa in Akananuru 257 on the summer road, vengai in Ainkurunuru 396 at the edge of his town.
links.teaches: Akananuru's adorning happens on the march and admires how she walks, while Ainkurunuru's is a pause that lets her rest before she enters his town as a guest, so the flowers in her hair move from a token of the road to a preparation for her reception.

links.note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving by stealth, pities her companions (அளியரோ அளியர் என் ஆயத்தோர்) who will grieve at the ball and anklets she left; Ainkurunuru 397's speaker sends word ahead to her companions (என் ஆயத்தோர்க்கே) that she is coming.
links.teaches: The companions whose grief the girl foresaw as she slipped away are the first she sends a message to on the way back, so the playmates frame the elopement at both ends, its first cost and its first news.

links.note: 373 wishes on the youth's mother the grief of weeping at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் இடும்பை); 398's speaker says that she herself weeps so at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் என்னினும்) but the town is lonelier still.
links.teaches: Read together, the curse in 373 turns out to be the speaker's own condition, wished on the other mother, and in 398 the same grief is no longer used against anyone but set beside the town's loss while she blesses the road.

links.note: Akananuru 195's mother asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?); Ainkurunuru 399 proposes the answer: the anklet-removal in his house, the wedding in ours.
links.teaches: The question Akananuru leaves to the diviner Ainkurunuru settles by dividing the rites between the two houses, which shows that which house received the couple was a matter of standing that families negotiated, not only a mother's anxiety.

links.note: Akananuru 369's foster mother fears the girl had her anklets removed without honour in a poor stranger's hut (சிலம்புடன் கழீஇ); Ainkurunuru 399 concedes the anklet-removal to the youth's house but claims the wedding for the girl's own.
links.teaches: The anklet-removal that Akananuru dreads as a rite done without the family is in Ainkurunuru granted to the other house on condition of a proper wedding at home, so the girl's people could accept the lost rite once the honour of the wedding was kept.

source_issues: 393 line 2: அண்கணாட்டி is a rare word whose sense is not fixed; read here as a name for the mother (the one addressed), and the verse is marked uncertain.
397 line 4: விரந்தநீர் is read as விரைந்த நீர் (you who hasten); the form may be a scribal variant.
Every colophon thurai in this decade is null; speakers in thurai_akam are inferred from the poems and the decade's title.
